summary: Discusses how three major bibliographic identifiers, ISBN, ISSN and SICI, can be used within the Uniform Resource Name framework. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2288 shows how three identifiers used for books and serial publications could fit the proposed URN syntax. It is a feasibility example, not an official standard for encoding those identifiers.

questions: how to use isbn as a urn
how to write an isbn as a urn
subtitle: How ISBN, ISSN and SICI identifiers can be written within the proposed URN framework.

tldr.problem: The URN framework needed to show that its syntax could accommodate established identifiers from other naming systems.
tldr.mechanism: This memo demonstrates URN forms for ISBNs, ISSNs and SICIs, and describes comparison rules and percent-encoding where needed.
tldr.outcome: The examples show feasibility only. RFC 2288 does not establish an official encoding standard for these identifiers.

facts.label: ISBN length
facts.value: 10 characters, final character may be X

facts.label: SICI identifiers
facts.value: Serial issues or contributions within an issue

today: RFC 2288 is an Informational memo published in February 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo describes feasibility rather than an official encoding standard.

sections.title: Purpose and Limits
sections.content:
Uniform Resource Names (URNs) need to support identifiers from existing naming systems. This memo tests that idea with the International Standard Book Number (ISBN), International Standard Serial Number (ISSN), and Serial Item and Contribution Identifier (SICI).

The authors state that these examples demonstrate feasibility only. They were not developed with the organizations responsible for the identifiers, and any official standard would need consultation with those organizations. The namespace identifiers shown in the examples are also illustrative choices.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo tests whether three existing identifiers fit the proposed URN syntax. It does not set an official rule for using them as URNs.

sections.title: A Name Is Not a Lookup Result
sections.content:
A URN identifies a resource; resolving the URN is a separate task. An ISSN can identify a serial publication as a whole, so returning every issue and article would not be a useful result. A resolver could instead provide a way to choose a specific issue or article.

An identified item may exist only in print. In that case, a resolver may provide information about where to obtain it, such as library holdings or a publisher. ISBNs and SICIs identify finite objects, but a resolver may still use a hierarchy to present them.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN identifies an item, but does not itself retrieve that item. A resolver may instead help a person find an issue, article, library copy or publisher.

sections.title: ISBNs for Book Editions
sections.content:
An ISBN identifies an edition of a book. It contains 10 digits, although the final character may be X. Its parts identify a publisher group, publisher, title, and a modulus 11 check digit. The memo's example is URN:ISBN:0-395-36341-1.

The memo says ISBN characters do not require percent-encoding in the URN identifier segment. Before comparing ISBN URNs, it recommends removing hyphens and converting any x to uppercase. ISBN assignment practices can differ between publishers and between formats or editions.
sections.plainLanguage: An ISBN identifies a book edition. For comparison, remove its hyphens and treat a final x as uppercase; the memo's proposed URN form needs no percent-encoding.

sections.title: ISSNs for Serial Publications
sections.content:
An ISSN identifies a serial publication as a whole, such as a journal or newspaper. Its form is NNNN-NNNN, and the last character may be uppercase X. The memo gives URN:ISSN:1046-8188 as an example.

For comparisons, the memo recommends removing the hyphen and converting x to uppercase. It notes that publication practices can differ about whether an item is a serial or a monograph, and when a new ISSN is assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: An ISSN identifies a continuing publication, not one particular issue. To compare ISSN URNs, remove the hyphen and use uppercase X if it appears.

sections.title: SICIs for Issues and Contributions
sections.content:
A SICI can identify an issue of a serial publication or a contribution within an issue, such as an article. It is constructed from information about the item, rather than assigned. Its parts can include the serial's ISSN, chronology, enumeration, a contribution segment and a control segment.

Some SICI characters are reserved or excluded in URN syntax, so they must be percent-encoded. The memo does not define lexical comparison rules for SICIs; it leaves matching to resolver systems because different SICIs can represent the same article.
sections.plainLanguage: A SICI can identify one issue or one contribution within an issue. Some of its characters need percent-encoding, and this memo leaves comparisons between SICIs to resolvers.

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content: The memo discusses identifier encoding, not resolution. It therefore does not address secure or authenticated resolution, checking the source or integrity of a URN, or intellectual property rights in identified items and resolver databases.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo covers how identifiers can be written as URNs. It does not define secure lookup or verify the origin of a URN.
